1: Data transformation and feature scaling. Lectures twenty three and twenty four plus lab twenty three and twenty four, using one real dataset: California Housing, with twenty thousand six hundred forty rows.
2: Today we have three ideas on one dataset. One, why transform? Skew, heavy tails and mixed units hide patterns and hurt models. Two, change the shape, with the log transform and Box Cox, and Yeo Johnson. Three, change the units, with standardisation, MinMax and robust scaling. In the lab we apply every method to all seven numeric features and compare the distribution before and after, with statistics, skew, kurtosis and outliers, and graphs, histogram, box plot and density. The key idea: transforming changes the shape, and scaling changes the units.
3: The dataset is California Housing from the nineteen ninety census. Twenty thousand six hundred forty block groups, seven numeric features to transform, two hundred seven missing values in total bedrooms to fill with the median, and population has a skew of four point nine four. The features are housing median age, total rooms, total bedrooms, population, households, median income in tens of thousands of dollars, and median house value in dollars. We do not transform longitude and latitude, which are a location and longitude is negative, nor the text column ocean proximity. And note that median house value is top coded at five hundred thousand and one, a real data quality quirk.
4: Lecture twenty three and twenty four. Why transform, log, Box Cox, scaling, and the impact on distribution.
5: Why transform? Four reasons. One, squashed plots: most points crowd into one corner, and the long tail stretches the axis. Two, model assumptions: linear and logistic regression, L D A and many tests work best with symmetric features and linear relationships. Three, false outliers: in a long tail, many outliers are just normal large values. The chart shows the raw features on a log axis, with ranges differing by a factor of ten thousand. Four, mixed units: years, counts and dollars in one model, and the biggest numbers dominate distances and gradients. Points one to three call for a transform, and point four calls for scaling.
6: Five of seven features are strongly right skewed. As a guide: absolute skew below point five is roughly symmetric, point five to one is a moderate skew, and above one is a strong skew. Population is four point nine four, total rooms four point one five, bedrooms three point four eight, and households three point four one: count data with long right tails. Housing median age is point zero six, already symmetric, so leave its shape alone.
7: Transforming versus scaling. A transform changes the shape. It is non linear, so big values are pulled in more than small ones. Skewness and kurtosis change, the order of values is kept, and examples are log, square root, Box Cox and Yeo Johnson. Scaling changes the units. It is linear: subtract a centre and divide by a spread. Skewness and kurtosis stay exactly the same, the features become comparable in size, and examples are standard, MinMax and robust. For skewed data, transform first, then scale.
8: The log transform: y equals log of one plus x. It compresses large values much more than small ones. The plus one keeps x equal to zero safe, and x must be at least zero. It turns multiplicative effects into additive ones, so equal ratios become equal steps. And it has a fixed strength: the same pull for every feature. For example, population of three becomes one point three nine, ten becomes two point four, one thousand becomes six point nine one, and thirty five thousand six hundred eighty two becomes ten point four eight. A twelve thousand times range becomes about nine units. A caution from our data: log over corrects the count features, with population skew going from four point nine four to minus one point oh four, and damages the symmetric housing median age, from point oh six to minus one point one four, creating five hundred fifty nine new I Q R outliers.
9: Box Cox lets the data choose the power lambda. Y equals x to the lambda minus one, divided by lambda, if lambda is not zero, and the log of x if lambda is zero. Lambda is chosen to make the result as close to normal as possible, by maximum likelihood. It requires every x to be positive. Data with zeros or negatives uses Yeo Johnson, the same idea for any real value. The power ladder from weaker to stronger: lambda one is no change in shape, point five is the square root, zero is the log, and minus one is the reciprocal. Our lambda values: housing median age point eight one, almost untouched, the counts point two two to point two five, between square root and log, and median income point oh nine, near log.
10: Three ways to scale. Standard scaler: z equals x minus mean divided by standard deviation, giving mean zero and standard deviation one. It is unbounded, so outliers stay far away and pull the mean and standard deviation. MinMax scaler: x minus min divided by max minus min, giving every value between zero and one. One extreme value sets the max and squeezes the rest. Robust scaler: x minus median divided by I Q R, giving median zero and I Q R one. The median and I Q R ignore extremes, so it is best with outliers. All three are linear: the histogram keeps its shape, and only the axis numbers change.
11: Measuring the impact on a distribution. Symmetry: check skewness, which should move toward zero. Tails: check kurtosis, where large positive values should shrink. Outliers: the I Q R rule count, where tail values should be pulled inside the whiskers. Shape: histogram and density, where one tall spike should become a bell. Spread: box plot, where boxes should be comparable across features. Always compare the number and the picture together. A statistic can hide a cap, a gap or two peaks that the graph reveals.

24: The MinMax trap: one extreme value sets the scale. The fraction of MinMax scaled population below point one is point nine six, the maximum population is thirty five thousand six hundred eighty two, and the median is eleven sixty six. So ninety six percent of population values fall below point one. The largest block group becomes one point zero, a typical block group with eleven sixty six people becomes point oh three, and the top four percent of rows occupy ninety percent of the zero to one range. The fix: transform first, or use robust scaler.
25: Step six: transform first, then scale. Power transformer with method box cox, and standardize equal to true, the default, does Box Cox plus standard scaler in one step. Every feature then has mean zero, standard deviation one, and absolute skew at most point one two. The population maximum falls from thirty point two five to seven point four seven. For models, fit on training data only, then transform the test data, so no test information leaks in.
26: Which method when? Strong right skew with all x positive: Box Cox, which brought all seven features to absolute skew at most point one two. Right skew with x at least zero, wanting something simple and interpretable: log one p, though counts over corrected to about minus one. Zeros or negative values: Yeo Johnson, needed for longitude, which is all negative. Already symmetric, absolute skew below point five: no transform, since log on age created five fifty nine outliers. Roughly normal, for P C A, regression or S V M: standard scaler. Need zero to one with few outliers: MinMax scaler, though ninety six percent of population was squeezed below point one. Many outliers or heavy tails: robust scaler. Tree models: usually none, because splits depend on order, not scale.
27: Transform the shape, then scale the units. Check skew before choosing. Box Cox adapts, log does not. Scaling never fixes skew. And robust beats MinMax when outliers exist. The lab notebook has exercises at the end.
